t: Install Ostler with a double-click, an editor extension, pip or uvx, or one command: no Rust and no config files. Ostler lets an AI assistant (Claude, Cursor, Codex) use a real web browser on your computer: read pages, research a topic with sources it actually read, and fill in web forms. You do not need Rust, Node or any code. Back to the README . Status: early (v0.2). v0.2.0 is released, so the download steps below work (macOS and Linux; Windows and Docker arrive in the next release, experimental). The VS Code Marketplace, crates.io and npm are not published yet ( INSTALL ).

A Mac or Linux computer (Windows and Docker arrive in the next release, experimental; see INSTALL ). Google Chrome ( download ). An AI app that supports MCP: Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf or Codex.

s: Path A: Claude Desktop on a Mac (one double-click)
t: Open the latest release and download the .mcpb file for your Mac ( aarch64 = Apple silicon M1 or newer, x86_64 = Intel). Double-click it. Claude Desktop shows an install prompt; click Install . Start a chat and ask: "Open https://example.com and tell me what the page says."

s: Path B: any supported app, one command
t: Open Terminal (Mac: press Cmd+Space, type Terminal) and paste: curl -fsSL https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/install.sh | sh ostler start ostler start finds the AI apps on your computer, connects Ostler to each one, checks that Chrome is there, and tells you what to restart. It backs up any file it changes, keeps your other settings, and is safe to run twice. To undo: ostler install --client <name> --uninstall ( ostler install --list shows the names). Then quit and reopen your AI app .

s: Path C: VS Code, Cursor or Windsurf extension
t: Search the extensions panel for Ostler (Open VSX for Cursor and Windsurf; the VS Code Marketplace listing is not published yet), install it, and Ostler appears as an MCP server. No terminal. It uses an ostler already on your PATH, or downloads the matching release once and checks its checksum. Commands: Ostler: Check setup , Ostler: Sign in to a website . Source: editors/vscode .

s: Path D: Python ( pip or uvx )
t: pip install ostler-mcp # adds the `ostler` command (use pipx or `uv tool install` to keep it isolated) ostler start Or with no install step, in any MCP client's config: command uvx , arguments ["--from", "ostler-mcp", "ostler", "serve"] . The package is the same Rust program inside a Python wheel (no Python code, nothing downloaded at run time). The name is ostler-mcp because ostler on PyPI is a different project.

s: Path E: one-click links for Cursor and VS Code
t: After installing the ostler command (Path B, first line), these links add it to the app: Add to Cursor Add to VS Code They assume ostler is on your PATH ; ostler start does not need that. The link formats follow the apps' published install-link schemes but have not been tested here.

Apps that show MCP prompts (Claude Desktop lists them under the + menu) offer five from Ostler: summarize a page, research with checked sources, fill in a form (review before sending), check my web page, compare pages. Pick one, fill in the blank, send.

For tasks behind a login, sign in once yourself: ostler login https://example.com/login A Chrome window opens. Sign in, then press Enter in Terminal. Then connect Ostler with that saved session: ostler install --client claude-desktop -- --profile-dir ~/.ostler/profile . Anyone who can read that folder can use your sign-in, so use it on your own computer only.

"Open this page and summarize it: <link>" "Research <topic>. Only use pages you actually read, and check every quote against the page." "Fill in the contact form on <link> with my name and email, then show me what you entered before submitting." "Check that the login page on my site still works after my change." For a safe practice page, run ostler fixtures and ask the assistant to fill in the form at http://127.0.0.1:8787/dependent.html. Nothing real is submitted.

ostler start --cautious connects Ostler so page requests that change things (form posts and similar) are blocked unless the assistant uses its confirmed submit step. It is stricter than normal and can also stop some sign-ins or buttons. Run ostler start again without the flag to go back.

you see meaning VERIFIED / NOT VERIFIED the quoted words were (or were not) found on a page the assistant actually read. It proves the words are there, not that they are true NOT READ the assistant cited a page it never opened gaps in evidence pages it could not read (paywall, bot check, blocked by the site's robots.txt, error) CHALLENGE: the site showed a CAPTCHA or "are you human" check. Ostler does not solve these UNMATCHED key a detail you gave matches no field on the form, so nothing was guessed NOT ACCEPTED the site rejected the form and says why

Ostler uses its own Chrome window, hidden by default. To sign in to a site once and reuse it, or to solve a CAPTCHA yourself, see Troubleshooting . Ostler does not solve CAPTCHAs and does not submit real forms unless you ask the assistant to. Your AI app may send what it reads to its own model provider. Ostler itself sends pages nowhere.
Run ostler doctor . Every failing check prints the exact fix. More in Troubleshooting .

Install, check, connect, then read and cite a demo page or fill a demo form, in five minutes. Install Ostler, check that it can drive Chrome, connect your agent, and try it on a demo page: read and cite a source, or fill a form. About five minutes. Note Status: v0.2, early. Ostler is tested against real Chrome and a real Qdrant server, but only on local fixtures, not the open web. A design review found real flaws and lists them openly with a fix order. Read what that means before relying on it.

You need Chrome or Chromium (Ostler drives a real browser) and Python 3.8+ (no Rust needed). pip install ostler-mcp No Python? Use the install script (macOS and Linux): curl -fsSL https://inamdarmihir.github.io/ostler/install.sh | sh . With Rust 1.89+ you can build from source: cargo install --git https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler ostler . Every option, and what is not published yet (npm, crates.io, Homebrew), is on the Install page.

ostler doctor ostler doctor launches Chrome, round-trips a page and, if you configured Qdrant, prints a memory report (sealing, key location, where embeddings are computed, isolation, transport) and checks that Qdrant is reachable. When something is wrong it prints the command that fixes it; ostler doctor --fix applies the safe ones (creating the config directory). With no config at all, memory is in-process for the session and nothing needs Qdrant or a key. See Troubleshooting if it does not pass.

ostler install --client claude-code # or claude-desktop | cursor | vscode | windsurf | codex That writes the entry into the client's config file with the binary's absolute path: it backs the file up first, keeps your other servers, refuses a malformed file and prints what changed ( --dry-run previews, --uninstall removes). ostler install --list shows every client. To only print a snippet instead, use ostler setup <client> . Prefer your own Chrome window? See "Use your own Chrome" on the Install page. Details for every client are in Use with your agent . After installing or rebuilding ostler , reconnect the MCP client (Claude Code: /mcp ; others: restart it) so it starts the new binary.

ostler fixtures # serves synthetic test pages at http://127.0.0.1:8787 Pick one. Nothing real is read or submitted; these are bundled test pages. Research with a checked quote. Ask your agent: Read http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-lock.html. Who designed the Kestrel Lock and when did it open? Cite every claim with cite and call evidence before answering. Ostler reads the page, accepts a quote that is on it, refuses one that is not, and lists any page it could not read. The full walk-through, with unedited output, is in Research with checked citations . Fill a form. Ask your agent: Open http://127.0.0.1:8787/dependent.html and fill in the shipping form for Ada Lovelace in Germany,
Bavaria. Ostler fills Country, watches State load, reads every value back, and reports what the page said.

ostler doctor # Chrome launches? Memory report; Qdrant reachable? Every failing check prints the command that fixes it ostler doctor --fix # apply only the safe fixes: create the config directory, chmod 600 an open key file ostler doctor explains launch failures (sandbox or root problems, a profile already in use, missing libraries, Chrome not installed) with a concrete command for each. --fix never creates keys, installs software, edits client configs or touches the network.

Easiest: ostler start finds the AI apps on your computer and connects Ostler to each. Or pick one: ostler install --list # clients and their config files ostler install --client claude-code # or claude-desktop | cursor | vscode | windsurf | codex This edits the client's config file for you: it refuses a file that is not valid JSON/TOML, makes a backup first, keeps your other servers and prints exactly what changed. Re-running it changes nothing; --dry-run previews and --uninstall removes the entry. Nothing else needs configuring: with no config at all, memory is in-process for the session and no Qdrant or key is involved.

Start Chrome yourself with a debugging port on loopback and a dedicated profile, then point Ostler at it: "/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome" --remote-debugging-port=9222 --remote-debugging-address=127.0.0.1 --user-data-dir=$HOME/.ostler/chrome-profile ostler doctor --cdp-url http://127.0.0.1:9222 ostler install --client claude-code -- --cdp-url http://127.0.0.1:9222 Only loopback is accepted. Ostler never opens the port for you, works in its own tab and leaves your browser running. While the port is open any local program can drive that Chrome, so use a dedicated profile.

macOS: tested locally. Linux: tested in CI. In containers or as root you may need OSTLER_NO_SANDBOX=1 , plus a larger /dev/shm ( --shm-size=1g ) for Chrome. See Troubleshooting . Windows (x86_64): builds and runs its test suite in CI; ships from the next release (v0.2.1). Experimental, with no day-to-day use yet. Docker (linux/amd64, linux/arm64): ships from the next release (v0.2.1). Browser: Chrome or Chromium only. If Chrome is in a non-standard place, set OSTLER_CHROME=/path/to/chrome or pass --chrome-path .
Rerun the same install command. install.sh replaces the binary in place. Then reconnect your MCP client (Claude Code: /mcp ; others: restart it) so it starts the new binary.

Run ostler install --client <name> --uninstall for each client you registered (it keeps your other servers and backs the file up). Delete the ostler binary ( ~/.local/bin/ostler , or ~/.cargo/bin/ostler ), and ~/.config/ostler and ~/.cache/ostler if you want the settings and the npx download gone. Memory lives in your Qdrant, not on disk here. ostler memory wipe --yes erases it, so run that first if you want it gone.

By default, nothing apart from the binary and, if you run ostler init , the config file ~/.config/ostler/config.toml (owner-only permissions). With sealed memory, a key file memory.key next to the config. Chrome uses a throwaway profile unless you pass --profile-dir . Ostler sends no telemetry.

install.sh is served from this site and verifies a checksum before installing; on a mismatch it installs nothing and runs nothing. It installs to ~/.local/bin by default ( OSTLER_INSTALL_DIR changes that, OSTLER_VERSION pins a version) and never edits your shell profile or your agent's config. You can read the script first: install.sh .

Add Ostler as an MCP browser to Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code or any MCP client, with a forms and a research workflow. Ostler is an MCP server over stdio. Any MCP client can launch it. ostler setup <client> prints the exact config, using this binary's absolute path . That avoids "command not found" when an app's PATH differs from your shell's. client command result Claude Code ostler setup claude --apply runs claude mcp add for you Codex ostler setup codex prints the block for ~/.codex/config.toml Cursor ostler setup cursor prints JSON for ~/.cursor/mcp.json VS Code ostler setup vscode prints JSON for .vscode/mcp.json anything else ostler setup json generic mcpServers JSON Only Claude

Code is applied automatically. Other clients' files are never modified: you paste or merge the printed snippet. Extra serve flags go after -- : ostler setup claude --apply -- --lean --tools forms Note Client config formats change between releases. If one of these does not load, check that client's current MCP documentation. The server itself only needs ostler serve on stdio.
ostler setup claude --apply # manual equivalent: claude mcp add ostler -- ostler serve Reconnect with /mcp after installing or rebuilding.
ostler setup codex Prints a block for ~/.codex/config.toml . Paste or merge it: [mcp_servers.ostler] command = "/absolute/path/to/ostler" args = ["serve"]
ostler setup cursor Prints JSON for ~/.cursor/mcp.json (or .cursor/mcp.json in a project): { "mcpServers" : { "ostler" : { "command" : "/absolute/path/to/ostler" , "args" : [ "serve" ] } } }

Easiest: install the Ostler extension from Open VSX (Cursor, Windsurf and other forks; the VS Code Marketplace listing is not published yet). It registers Ostler as an MCP server, uses an ostler on your PATH or downloads and checks the release once, and adds Ostler: Check setup and Ostler: Sign in to a website . Source: editors/vscode . Or by hand: ostler setup vscode Prints JSON for .vscode/mcp.json . VS Code uses a servers key and an explicit transport type: { "servers" : { "ostler" : { "type" : "stdio" , "command" : "/absolute/path/to/ostler" , "args" : [ "serve" ] } } }

Any MCP client can launch Ostler from the Python package ostler-mcp (it carries the same binary): { "mcpServers" : { "ostler" : { "command" : "uvx" , "args" : [ "--from" , "ostler-mcp" , "ostler" , "serve" ] } } } pip install ostler-mcp instead puts the ostler command on your PATH. Use pipx or uv tool install to keep it isolated.

ostler setup json prints the common mcpServers shape. The only requirement is that the client starts ostler serve and speaks MCP over stdio. ostler serve should print one ready line on stderr and wait; stdout carries only MCP messages. Building your own agent in Python? See LangChain, LlamaIndex and AutoGen for tested code. Keep one Ostler session open for the whole task, or cite will not see what read fetched.

For research with citations: search (or start from known URLs), then open_many with a query to read the best passages of up to 10 pages. read with a query to go deeper on one page; follow links or extract tables and lists. cite every quote you intend to use. Only VERIFIED quotes go in the answer. evidence before answering: it lists the verified citations and the pages that could not be read, which the answer should name as gaps. A prompt that works: "Research X. Cite every claim with cite ; call evidence before answering and list what you could not read." For reading or testing a page: navigate opens the page and lists its interactive elements; snapshot returns the page as text (pass a

heading's ref to read one section). look returns a screenshot with numbered click targets, which helps when a cookie banner or modal is in the way. click , type , press and wait_for act on the page; screenshot captures the result. Page text arrives fenced as untrusted, so instructions inside a page are data, not commands. For forms: navigate returns the page's interactive elements. form_inspect returns typed fields and shows what memory knows about this form. form_fill with {label: value} for what you know; add auto: "required" to fill the rest from memory. form_submit , then read the status: Submitted , Advanced (next step: repeat 2 to 4), or NOT ACCEPTED with the page's validation
messages. ostler inspect <url> prints the form model as JSON for debugging.

s: Control what the agent sees and can do
t: flag effect --tools core|forms|all which tools the agent sees (12, 16 or 21). Fewer tools means less schema in every turn --allow-domain example.com (repeatable) only that domain and subdomains, every request and WebSockets included; example.com:8443 pins a port --require-confirm-submit form_submit fails unless the agent passes confirm=true , so a human can approve --upload-dir DIR (repeatable) file fields may be filled from this directory; without it uploads are refused --block-private-networks with no allowlist, refuse loopback, private, metadata and internal hosts --accept-dialogs answer the page's confirm() and prompt() with OK; they are dismissed by default --lean lower memory; no

s: Control what the agent sees and can do
t: images, fonts or media --profile-dir DIR persistent Chrome profile (keeps logins); one profile per server --headed visible browser, for watching it work and for wait_for_human --learn save non-sensitive values typed after an accepted submit (off by default) The full flag list is on the Configuration and CLI page, and the reasoning is in the Security model .

Cookies and logins carry across tabs. The context tool is a small key/value notepad that every tab and every later call can read, for things like "applicant = Ada, order id = 4471". It survives a browser restart. Popups arrive as tabs under the same domain policy.
If another agent, rather than a coding agent, should hand Ostler a form, use A2A instead of MCP.

Use Ostler's tools from three Python agent frameworks: tested code, real output, and the one-session rule for cite. Ostler is an MCP server, so any agent framework with an MCP adapter can use its browser, research and form tools. This page shows the three popular Python frameworks, with the code that was run and the output it produced. What was tested, and what was not. Each snippet below was run against Ostler 0.2.0 and the bundled demo page ( ostler fixtures ): the adapter connects over stdio, loads the tools, and calls read then cite directly. No language model was in the loop , so the step that hands the tools to an agent is shown as documented usage and marked as not run.

s: The one rule: keep one session open
t: cite only accepts a quote from a page that read fetched in the same Ostler session . A session is one running Ostler process. Adapters differ in whether they keep it: framework default behaviour what to do LangChain ( langchain-mcp-adapters ) client.get_tools() starts a new Ostler process per tool call, so cite returns NOT READ open client.session("ostler") and use load_mcp_tools(session) LlamaIndex ( llama-index-tools-mcp ) BasicMCPClient starts a new process per call, so cite returns NOT READ open an mcp.ClientSession yourself and pass it to McpToolSpec AutoGen ( autogen-ext[mcp] ) McpWorkbench as a context manager keeps one session use async with McpWorkbench(params) Both failures were

s: The one rule: keep one session open
t: observed, not assumed: the NOT READ reply is NOT READ: <url> was not read in this session ... call read first . It is Ostler refusing to certify a quote from a page it did not read in that session, which is the point of cite . Run the agent inside the async with block; when the block exits, the Ostler process and its Chrome end and the read history is gone. Every example assumes ostler is on your PATH (see install ) and the demo pages are being served with ostler fixtures . --tools research pins the 21 research-profile tools; use --tools all for all 30 ( profiles ).

pip install langchain-mcp-adapters # tested: 0.3.2, with mcp 1.30.0 import asyncio from langchain_mcp_adapters.client import MultiServerMCPClient from langchain_mcp_adapters.tools import load_mcp_tools URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-lock.html" client = MultiServerMCPClient({"ostler": {"transport": "stdio", "command": "ostler", "args": ["serve", "--tools", "research"]}}) async def main(): async with client.session("ostler") as session: # one session = one Ostler process tools = {t.name: t for t in await load_mcp_tools(session)} print("loaded:", len(tools), list(tools)[:8]) await tools["read"].ainvoke({"url": URL}) for quote in ["It opened in 1887 and was designed by Marta

Ilves", "Tomas Reyes designed the Kestrel Lock in 1887"]: r = await tools["cite"].ainvoke({"url": URL, "quote": quote}) print(r[0]["text"][:90].replace("\n", " ")) asyncio.run(main()) Output (the second quote is a decoy that is not on the page): loaded: 21 ['navigate', 'snapshot', 'read', 'click', 'type', 'press', 'hover', 'scroll'] VERIFIED [1] <page_content untrusted="true">http://127.0.0.1:8787/packs/research/kestrel-l NOT VERIFIED: these words are not on <page_content untrusted="true">The Kestrel Lock</page Tool results come back as a list of content blocks, so the text is r[0]["text"] . To hand the tools to an agent, keep the agent call inside the same async with block. Not run (no

model available here; langchain and a model package are extra installs): from langchain.agents import create_agent async with client.session("ostler") as session: agent = create_agent("anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5", await load_mcp_tools(session)) await agent.ainvoke({"messages": "Who designed the Kestrel Lock? Read pages, check each quote against them, and report what could not be read, with real tool output. Ostler checks a quotation against the text of a page it actually read in this session, and lists the pages it could not read. An agent using read , cite and evidence can then answer with only the claims that were verified, and say plainly what it could not check. It runs on your machine, in your Chrome, from any MCP client such as Claude Code, Codex or Cursor. What this does not do. cite proves that the words are on the page. It does not prove that the claim is true, that the page is a good source, or that the agent quoted in context. Quote matching is not fact-checking.

Three tools carry it. They are in the research profile; --tools research pins them, and the default --tools auto reveals them after the first read . All 32 tools are in the tools reference . step tool what it does 1 read Opens a page and returns the best passages for your query , with a fetch time and a content hash. The page text is stored for this session. 2 cite Takes a url and a quote (12 or more characters). Returns VERIFIED with a link a person can open to check the words, or NOT VERIFIED , NOT READ or TOO SHORT . 3 evidence Lists verified citations, pages read but not cited, and gaps: paywall, bot wall, robots.txt refusal, HTTP error, empty page. Call it before answering. open_many

reads up to 10 URLs at once in a scratch tab and obeys robots.txt. search finds pages to read; it needs a provider ( OSTLER_SEARXNG_URL , or OSTLER_SEARCH_PROVIDER=brave with OSTLER_BRAVE_API_KEY ) and has been tested against mock servers only.

How keys become fields, how values are verified by read-back, and what submit results mean. Ostler's form engine is built so the model states intent once and the engine does the mechanics: it resolves each key to a field, fills in order, lets dependent controls appear, reads every value back, and reports what actually happened.

form_inspect returns typed fields: kind, label, required, options, pattern, current value, and any error. It also lists submit controls and says what memory knows about this form. form_fill takes {label | name | ref: value} for the whole form. form_submit clicks the submit or next control and reports the outcome. Dependent dropdowns, multi-step wizards, input masks, comboboxes, shadow DOM and same-origin iframes are handled inside these calls. See the tools reference for parameters.

s: How a key becomes a field
t: Keys are resolved in this order: exact ref, then name or id, then label, then fuzzy label. A key can match by ref, name, label or fuzzy label, and keys are resolved against every visible field once, so an ambiguous key cannot win by elimination. Ambiguity is reported, never guessed. If two fields match equally well, the report says ambiguous and asks for the ref. email finds "E-mail address", because a key equal to a run of the label's words written together matches, but two equally plausible fields are still refused. A key that matches nothing is UNMATCHED . It is not dropped silently, and the fill report only counts as OK if no key was unmatched. Forms re-mounted by a framework are

s: How a key becomes a field
t: followed.

The engine converts the value for the field before writing it: you send field written "Germany" select the option index for that option text "March 5, 2001" date 2001-03-05 "3:30 PM" time 15:30 03/04/2024 date refused as ambiguous (day-first or month-first), so the agent must say which Fields are filled in document order and the form is re-inspected after every field , so a dependent control (State after Country) appears before it is needed.

After writing a field, the engine reads the value back from the live page and compares it by field type. A value the page rewrote or cleared fails. A datetime-local must read back as the requested instant. A combobox must show the option you asked for. A longer option that merely contains it is a mismatch ("United States" versus "United States Minor Outlying Islands"), and the in-page picker only picks an exact, normalised option label, listing the options otherwise. Values the page legitimately reformats, such as (555) 123-4567 , are reported as reformatted , not as errors. Only exact matches and genuine reformatting pass. form_fill reports unsettled (a count) when the page was still busy

at the end of the fill, so the verdicts can be treated with care. Typed input is tried first, because it fires the same events a user would. If the page rejects it (masked or framework-controlled inputs), the engine retries with the native value setter plus events. Fills also send one harmless keyup , because some date pickers learn the text only from that event.

Just before clicking submit, form_submit re-reads the fields it verified and reports any the page cleared or rewrote in between as CHANGED BEFORE SUBMIT . This was added after a date picker was reported verified and then submitted empty.

result meaning Submitted the page accepted it: a new URL, or new confirmation text appeared after the click (for example a form that posts in the background and says "Thanks!" in place) Advanced the page moved to the next step of a wizard; repeat inspect, fill, submit NOT ACCEPTED the page reported problems, and the page's own messages follow SERVER ERROR the site answered the submit with an HTTP error (4xx/5xx) and showed no validation messages. The data may or may not have been stored: do not report it as submitted and do not retry blindly; check with snapshot or ask the user Nothing changed the form stayed put and said nothing visible. Check with snapshot ; do not resubmit blindly,

because it may have gone through With several forms on a page, form_submit with no form or control submits the form form_fill last filled; if none was filled it refuses and lists the forms rather than guessing the first. A thank-you page that still has an optional input (a newsletter box, a search) counts as Submitted , not Advanced , unless something on it is required, it has a step counter, or it has a "next" button.

Fields marked invalid only by colour (a red border, outline or glow, or red message text with no ARIA or class) and floating toasts or banners are reported as field and page errors. An error that was already on a field before the fill is flagged as possibly stale. An error message belongs to the field it follows, not to every field sharing a wrapper, and Bootstrap 3 .help-block is help text unless the group is .has-error .

Only real action buttons are submit candidates. The header's "Search" button, anything inside header , nav or role=search , and type-less buttons whose label says nothing about submitting ("Show tips") do not count.

Calendar date pickers on read-only inputs are handled heuristically: when a text field is read-only and the value is a date, the engine opens the popup, navigates months and clicks the day. It fails with a reason, not silently, when no popup or navigation is found. The heuristic looks for a month header, previous and next controls and day cells. Dropdown-only and year-only pickers are not handled.

Two tools help when a form is not obvious: look returns a screenshot with every clickable element boxed and numbered, and a legend such as e6 button "Send" -> submits the form . snapshot with a heading's ref reads just that section. A CAPTCHA, hCaptcha, Turnstile or "verify you are human" wall is reported with a CHALLENGE: line at the top of the result. The agent should stop retrying and ask you; with --headed , wait_for_human waits while you complete it. Ostler never solves or bypasses these ( ADR-0009 ).

Cross-origin iframes and closed shadow roots are invisible to the injected runtime. 2FA, CAPTCHA solving and anti-bot evasion are out of scope. Fill on very large forms (thousands of fields) is slow, because every key re-reads the form. It has been evaluated on local fixtures, not on the open web. See Benchmarks .

Ostler is a form-filling browser for an agent working on your behalf, on one machine. It is the wrong tool when: The site walls off automation. CAPTCHA, Cloudflare/Turnstile, "verify you are human" pages and search-engine bot checks are reported with a CHALLENGE: line and handed to a person. Ostler never solves or bypasses them, and it is not built to avoid detection: there is no stealth patching, fingerprint spoofing, residential proxy or IP rotation. A site that blocks headless or datacenter Chrome will block Ostler. --headed plus a persistent --profile-dir lets you pass a check once; it does not make a bot wall go away. You need scale. Each server drives one local Chrome (tabs share its

cookies and profile). It is not a remote or cloud browser farm, not a crawler, and not meant for bulk scraping or high-volume account creation. More sessions means more servers, each with its own profile and its own memory use (see Benchmarks ). The flow needs an identity Ostler does not have. There is no mailbox, phone number, SMS/OTP receiver or authenticator: one-time codes, email-link verification, passkeys, hardware keys and 2FA prompts need a person. Passwords and card numbers are never read back or remembered; sensitive fields are refused and the agent is told to ask you. It does not create accounts on your behalf out of thin air. The page is outside what the injected runtime can see.

Cross-origin iframes (many hosted card fields), closed shadow roots, canvas-drawn UIs, native OS dialogs and file pickers, and desktop apps are not reachable. A control that stays disabled until a person scrolls or hovers is reported as disabled rather than worked around. A wrong submit is expensive and nobody is checking. Ostler verifies every value by reading it back and refuses to call a submit a success without evidence, but it cannot know whether a form means what it says. For payments, legal acceptance and anything irreversible, run with --require-confirm-submit and review the result yourself. When Ostler cannot finish, it says which field and why (rejected value with the page's own
message, hidden or disabled control, key not found) and points at screenshot for the element; it does not report a partial fill as done.
The reasoning, with the alternatives that were rejected, is in ADR-0004 (injected runtime) and ADR-0005 (form model and verification). A summary is on the Architecture page.

What is stored, what sealing hides and does not, local embeddings, per-tenant tokens. Memory is optional. Browsing and form filling need no account and no key. When you turn it on, Ostler saves facts you told it, which fact fills which field on which site, and what went wrong on a form, in your own Qdrant . This page is exact about what is stored, what is encrypted, and what is not hidden. The sealing, local-embedding and per-tenant-token features below are described in the changelog's Unreleased section: they are on main and not in a tagged release yet. Unreleased

Three Qdrant collections, multi-tenant through a tenant payload index: collection holds never holds ostler_profile facts you saved ( email , company , …) passwords, card numbers, anything that looks sensitive ostler_playbooks per site and form: which fact fills which field, with wins, losses and last verified time the values themselves ostler_episodes what went wrong on a form, so it is not repeated secrets Ostler sends no telemetry. Disk holds nothing by default, apart from a Chrome profile if you pass --profile-dir , and the config and key files described below. Secrets are refused by the memory API (password, token and card-like keys, and card-number-like values), sensitive fields are

never auto-filled from memory nor stored by --learn , and sensitive values are masked in tool output. Detection is heuristic (names, autocomplete tokens, digit patterns): a secret stored under an innocuous key with an innocuous value will not be caught. Learned values never overwrite facts you saved. --learn is off by default. Ostler records how forms were filled automatically (structure only), but stores your data only when you opt in with --learn or call memory_remember .

Five places data can travel. Only the last two involve Qdrant, and only if you turn memory on. step where it goes what crosses what you control Browsing Chrome on your machine talks directly to the sites you visit. The page requests Chrome makes. Ostler sends no telemetry. --allow-domain limits every request the browser makes; --profile-dir decides whether logins persist. Tool output to your agent Over stdio to the MCP client that launched Ostler (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code). Page text, the values read back from form fields, and verification reports. Sensitive values are masked in tool output, but detection is heuristic. Your client decides what happens next. A client normally

forwards tool output to its model provider , so treat anything a tool returns as visible to that provider and check the client's own privacy settings. Search The SearXNG instance or Brave API you configure for search . The search query. Without a provider configured, search sends nothing. Embeddings By default, Qdrant Cloud Inference. With --embeddings ollama , your own machine. Unreleased With cloud inference, the field text to be embedded. --embeddings ollama keeps text local. Stored memory Your Qdrant. Facts you saved, playbooks and episodes. Sealed on your machine before upload by default. Unreleased --seal , --embeddings , --isolation ; memory_forget deletes. Secrets are the part to be

careful about. Memory refuses password-, token- and card-like keys and card-number-like values, but that check is a heuristic: a secret saved under an innocuous key and value would not be caught, and it would then also be part of what a later tool call returns to your agent.

s: Sealing: encrypt before it reaches Qdrant
t: With memory in Qdrant, payloads are sealed on your machine by default ( --seal auto ). Unreleased Fact values, descriptions, playbooks and episodes are encrypted with AES-256-GCM , with the point id bound in as associated data. Site names, field labels, profile keys and fingerprints are replaced by keyed hashes (HMAC-SHA-256) , and point ids are keyed too, so filters still work but the server cannot test guesses ("passport number") against what it stores. Episodes are redacted before they are embedded or stored: emails, runs of four or more digits (phones, PIN codes, card numbers) and URL query strings are masked, in addition to the values the agent typed. The key lives in OSTLER_MEMORY_KEY

s: Sealing: encrypt before it reaches Qdrant
t: or an owner-only memory.key next to the config file, created atomically on the first start. That start only creates a key after Qdrant was reached and holds no sealed memory for your tenant; with Qdrant down it refuses (start Qdrant, restore a backup with ostler memory key import , or pass --allow-new-key for a genuine first-time setup). Back it up: there is no recovery. If you lose it, sealed memory is unreadable. --seal on forces it; --seal off opts out (and ostler doctor and serve warn that anyone who can read your Qdrant can then read your saved facts and the sites you use).

s: What is hidden, and what is not
t: someone who can read your Qdrant (operator, leaked key, backup) sees Fact values and descriptions encrypted Playbooks and episodes (contents) encrypted; episodes are also redacted of emails and numbers Site names, field labels, profile keys, fingerprints keyed hashes only The vector visible. With --embeddings cloud , the field text is sent to Qdrant Cloud Inference to be embedded, and vectors of labels reveal roughly what they say. Use --embeddings ollama to keep text local Tenant name visible Win and loss counters, timing, point counts visible The key is, in order of precedence, the OSTLER_MEMORY_KEY variable, or the store chosen by key_store ( OSTLER_KEY_STORE ): file (default, owner-only

s: What is hidden, and what is not
t: memory.key ) or keychain (macOS Keychain / Linux Secret Service). Unreleased ostler memory key export --yes-print and ostler memory key import back it up and restore it.

Memory saved before sealing was on is invisible until you run: ostler config set seal on ostler memory seal Saved facts are copied into sealed form and read back to check them before the old plaintext points are deleted, so it is safe to interrupt and run again. Learned skills and episodes from that time are dropped and relearned.

By default Ostler embeds text with Qdrant Cloud Inference ( sentence-transformers/all-minilm-l6-v2 , 384 dimensions). To keep the text on your machine, embed locally with Ollama: Unreleased ostler serve --embeddings ollama --embedding-model <model> --embedding-dim <dims> --embeddings where text is embedded notes cloud (default) inside Qdrant Cloud Inference needs Inference enabled on the cluster. Field text is sent to Qdrant. Covered by request-shape tests; not run against a live Cloud cluster by the maintainers ollama on your machine, through an Ollama server only vectors reach Qdrant. --embedding-url defaults to http://127.0.0.1:11434 ( OSTLER_EMBEDDING_URL ); set --embedding-model and

--embedding-dim to match the model. Remote plain- http embedders are refused dev-hash on your machine, deterministic hash not semantic. Exact-key and autocomplete lookups work; fuzzy meaning does not. For open-source Qdrant development Exact signals need no vectors: lookups by playbook mapping and autocomplete token use payload filters.

Plain http:// to a non-loopback Qdrant is refused , because the API key and facts would cross the network unencrypted. --allow-insecure-qdrant ( OSTLER_ALLOW_INSECURE_QDRANT ) overrides it for links already protected by a VPN or tunnel. Unreleased If Qdrant fails twice in a row (transport error or 5xx), lookups are skipped for 30 seconds and tool results start with Note: memory is unavailable (...); continuing without it. Requests time out after 4 seconds.

By default all tenants share three collections, separated by a tenant filter in every query. A leaked admin key exposes every tenant in that mode. For stronger separation: Unreleased --isolation collection gives each tenant its own collections. ostler memory token mints a JWT that Qdrant itself limits to those collections, read-write or --read-only , and expiring. A leaked client token then exposes one tenant, not the cluster. Qdrant must run with service.jwt_rbac: true , and an admin must create the collections first. # 1. as admin: create alice's collections (`ostler memory list` does it) export QDRANT_URL=https://<cluster>.cloud.qdrant.io:6333 QDRANT_API_KEY=<admin key> export

OSTLER_ISOLATION=collection OSTLER_TENANT=alice ostler memory list # 2. mint a token for alice (30 days by default; add --read-only for search-only) ostler memory token --days 30 # 3. give alice the token instead of the admin key # QDRANT_API_KEY=<token> with --isolation collection --tenant alice Tested on a real Qdrant 1.20: another tenant's collections answer 403, and expired, forged and read-only tokens are refused. Qdrant 1.20 rejects the older per-point payload claim as deprecated, so isolation is per collection . Not covered: the default shared isolation shares collections, so a leaked admin key exposes every tenant, and collection isolation needs jwt_rbac and an admin who creates the
collections. Over A2A , all conversations share one tenant; run one server per tenant if callers must not see each other's profile.

For a field, in order of reliability: the form's own playbook mapping; an exact autocomplete -token match against your facts (payload filter, no vectors); a playbook from a similar form on the same site (a redesign or sibling form); semantic vector search. form_fill with auto: "required" fills what memory can supply and reports the rest. Semantic matches need a margin over the runner-up and never apply to labels about other people. Playbooks persist only exact (playbook or autocomplete ) matches.

Ostler needs no model to judge whether a fill worked: the browser reads every value back and the page accepts or rejects the submit, so every outcome is ground truth. step what happens Qdrant feature recall exact form first; after a redesign, mappings transfer from a similar form on the same site with the same label keyword-array filter on labels_norm and host , tenant index rank proven, recently verified skills beat stale or failing ones Query API prefetch and a score-boosting formula (similarity, smoothed win rate and exp_decay on verified_ts ) reinforce verified fields on accepted submits add wins per mapping integer payload indexes demote a mapping that loses more than it wins is dropped

forget ostler memory prune --days 90 removes stale, unproven skills; serve also forgets those not verified for 180 days on start ( --retain-days , 0 keeps them). Saved facts never expire range filter on verified_ts On a scripted site with redesigned forms, correct suggestions went from 1 to 8 of 10 fillable fields, with zero wrong fills in both conditions. That is a synthetic fixture, not real sites ( ADR-0008 ).

ostler memory list # saved facts ostler memory remember email you@example.com ostler memory forget email ostler memory skills # what was learned: wins, losses, trusted mappings ostler memory prune --days 90 ostler memory seal # re-save pre-sealing memory sealed ostler memory key export --yes-print # back up the sealing key ostler memory token # per-tenant JWT (see above) ostler memory wipe --yes # delete everything for this tenant No Qdrant? ostler init --local (or ostler config set memory local ) keeps memory in one file, memory.local , next to your config. It survives restarts, needs no server, and the whole file is encrypted with the same memory key as sealed Qdrant memory (AES-256-GCM,

written atomically, safe to use from serve and ostler memory at once). Embeddings stay on your machine: local word hashing by default (finds shared words, not meaning), or --embeddings ollama for semantic search. Back up the key; lost, the file cannot be read. --seal off stores plain JSON instead. Just trying things out: ostler memory --memory ephemeral list keeps memory in-process and loses it on exit.

you want you need browsing and form filling only nothing memory, no server, kept across sessions ostler init --local (encrypted file on this machine), no keys memory, trying it out --memory ephemeral (in-process, lost on exit), no keys memory on Qdrant Cloud cluster URL and API key, with Inference enabled on the cluster memory on self-hosted Qdrant URL (plus key if you set one) and --embeddings dev-hash , or --embeddings ollama for semantic search See Security model for the threat-model rows on secrets, cross-user exposure and anyone who can read your Qdrant.

Two kinds of older sealed points need one command, ostler memory seal , which is safe to repeat and copies before it deletes: v1 blobs (written by early builds) are no longer read: they did not authenticate the clear fields. serve , memory list and the other commands stop with the command to run; the upgrade opens them once with your key and saves them as v2 . Keys saved under an older normalisation (emoji-only keys, decomposed accents) sit at a different point than today's lookup asks for. The same command re-files them under the current key and removes the stray copy, without overwriting a newer fact. On Linux, key_store = keychain needs a running Secret Service (gnome-keyring, KWallet).
Without one Ostler stops with the reason and ostler config set key_store file ; it never falls back by itself, so the key is never half in a keyring and half on disk.

Config file, environment variables, every serve and a2a flag. Settings come from, in order: command-line flag, then environment variable, then the config file, then the default. One path per setting, so what ostler serve does is what ostler doctor tested.

ostler init Asks for a Qdrant URL and API key (skip both for no memory), a tenant name, and whether to enable --learn and --lean . It writes the config file with owner-only permissions and immediately tests the connection. Non-interactively: ostler init --qdrant-url https://<cluster>.cloud.qdrant.io --qdrant-api-key "$KEY" --tenant alice The :6333 port is added to Qdrant Cloud URLs for you. If the connection test fails the settings are still saved, so you can fix one value instead of retyping everything: ostler config show # key is masked ostler config set qdrant_url http://localhost:6333 ostler config unset learn ostler config path # ~/.config/ostler/config.toml

~/.config/ostler/config.toml (or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME , or the path in OSTLER_CONFIG ): key environment variable meaning qdrant_url QDRANT_URL Qdrant REST endpoint qdrant_api_key QDRANT_API_KEY Qdrant API key (secret; file is 0600 ) tenant OSTLER_TENANT isolates users sharing a cluster (default default ) memory OSTLER_MEMORY auto (on if a URL is set), qdrant , local (encrypted file, no server), ephemeral , off embeddings OSTLER_EMBEDDINGS cloud (Qdrant Cloud Inference), ollama (local) or dev-hash embedding_model OSTLER_EMBEDDING_MODEL Cloud Inference model (default sentence-transformers/all-minilm-l6-v2 , 384 dims) qdrant_on_disk OSTLER_QDRANT_ON_DISK keep vectors on disk: less RAM per user

learn OSTLER_LEARN save non-sensitive values typed after an accepted submit (off by default) lean OSTLER_LEAN lower memory use; no images in screenshots tools OSTLER_TOOLS core , forms or all Other environment variables used by the code: OSTLER_SEAL , OSTLER_ISOLATION , OSTLER_MEMORY_KEY , OSTLER_EMBEDDING_URL , OSTLER_EMBEDDING_DIM , OSTLER_ALLOW_INSECURE_QDRANT , OSTLER_RETAIN_DAYS , OSTLER_KEY_STORE , OSTLER_ALLOW_NEW_KEY (same as --allow-new-key : let a first start create the sealing key while Qdrant cannot be checked), OSTLER_VERBOSE , OSTLER_CHROME , OSTLER_NO_SANDBOX , OSTLER_A2A_BIND and OSTLER_A2A_TOKEN . All 32 MCP tools: browse, read and cite, search, extract, forms and memory, with parameters and profiles. Ostler exposes 32 MCP tools in five profiles. --tools auto|core|forms|research|all (or OSTLER_TOOLS ) controls how many the agent sees. The default, auto , starts with the 16 core tools (4.9 KB of schema), adds the research tools after the first read or search , and adds the form and memory tools once a page shows form fields. The server sends tools/list_changed , the result names the new tools, and every tool stays callable even if a client never refreshes its list. The full set is about 9.7 KB of schema, roughly 2.7k tokens on every turn, and a test keeps it under 11 KB. Tool output is

terse by default (verified fields are named once, no timings or fingerprints); --verbose brings the debug detail back. profile tools count auto (default) core, growing to research, forms and memory as the session needs them 15 to 30 core browse, read , tabs and context tools 15 forms core plus the form tools 19 research core plus the research tools 21 all everything, including memory and stats 30 Page-derived text in results (page content, titles, URLs, dialog text, the look legend) is wrapped in <page_content untrusted="true"> . The server instructions tell the model not to follow it. See Security model .

Open a URL. Returns page state with interactive elements, so no separate snapshot call is needed. parameter type notes url string, required observe interactive | full | none default interactive It reports the HTTP status ( Navigated (HTTP 404) ) with a plain-language reason, labels PDFs, downloads and redirects to a sign-in page, and explains navigation errors. A CAPTCHA or "verify you are human" page produces a CHALLENGE: line at the top. On a search-results URL whose visible text matches fewer than about half of the query's words, it adds a Warning: results do not seem to match the query .

Read the page as text with element refs ( e1 , e2 , …). Use delta to see only changes. Pass the ref of a heading to read just that section. parameter type notes mode full | delta | interactive ref string limit to a subtree max_chars integer Long text is split into several lines with an explicit … [N more chars cut] marker. Text a person cannot see is left out and counted.

Read a page for research (opens url if given). With query : only the best passages, ranked locally with BM25 and MMR, so a page costs a few hundred tokens instead of the whole text. Without: the start of the page. Only pages read this session can be cited. parameter type notes url string opens it first; omit to read the current tab query string what you are looking for k integer passages, default 5, max 12 max_chars integer default 8000 The header names the page, its size, fetch time and content hash, and flags what a reader must know first: PAYWALL , CHANGED (the page differs from an earlier read; earlier citations from it are re-checked), the page's own paging text ( showing 1-5 of 13 ),
and ATTENTION when the page contains text aimed at an AI. A bot wall, robots.txt refusal, HTTP error or empty page is NOT READ and is recorded as a gap, never as a source.

Click an element by ref. The result ends with a Result: line: navigated, popup opened as tab tN , page updated, or no visible change. parameter type notes ref string, required observe delta | full | none default delta
Move the pointer over an element by ref (opens menus and tooltips). parameter type notes ref string, required observe delta | full | none default delta

Scroll an element into view ( ref ) or the page ( direction ). Reports the position as scrolled/max, so the agent knows when it has reached the end of an infinite list. parameter type notes ref string element to bring into view direction up | down | top | bottom amount integer pixels observe delta | full | none default delta
Type into an element by ref, replacing its content. parameter type notes ref string, required text string, required submit boolean press Enter after observe delta | full | none default delta
Press a key, for example Enter , Tab , Escape , Control+a . parameter type notes key string, required observe delta | full | none default delta

Wait until text appears or disappears, or a CSS selector shows, or just pause for ms milliseconds (max 10000). parameter type notes text string wait for it to appear text_gone string wait for it to disappear selector string CSS selector timeout_ms integer ms integer plain pause

A CAPTCHA or verification wall is blocking the page: wait for the user to complete it in the browser window. Needs --headed . Ostler never solves these itself. parameter type notes timeout_s integer default 120, max 600
Capture a PNG of the page or one element. parameter type notes ref string one element full_page boolean

See where to click: a screenshot with every clickable element boxed and numbered by its ref, plus a legend saying what each does (type here, submits the form, error, …). Use the refs with click , type and fill_field . parameter type notes max integer Boxes come from DOM geometry and are coloured by role: green submits, blue inputs, purple links, red has an error. Elements hidden under a cookie banner, modal or sticky bar are left out and counted, so the agent closes the overlay first. It covers only the visible viewport. The overlay is removed afterwards. With --lean , screenshots omit images.
Go back in history. Takes no parameters. At the start of a tab's history it says so instead of landing on about:blank .
Manage tabs. They share cookies and the context tool. Popups open as new tabs. parameter type notes action list | new | switch | close , required tab string tab id, for example t2 url string for new

Find Ostler tools without listing them all: names, one-line descriptions or full input schemas for any tool, listed or not. parameter type notes query string words that must appear in the name or description detail string names , brief (default) or full

Notes shared by every tab and later calls: get , set , delete , list . Keep short facts, not page dumps. Survives a browser restart. parameter type notes action get | set | delete | list , required key string value string
Built around one contract: an answer can only contain what was read and verified. See the Cookbook for the workflow.

Check a quote against a page read this session. VERIFIED returns the page's exact words and a #:~:text= link a person can open to check them. NOT READ (the page was never read), NOT VERIFIED (with the closest text on the page) and TOO SHORT are errors: do not use that claim. Markdown on either side is ignored, so **1887** and [Marta Ilves](/m) still verify. parameter type notes url string, required a page read with read or open_many quote string, required words from the page, 12+ characters; ... marks an omission

What the agent has read and may state: verified citations, citations made stale by a changed page, pages read but not cited, and the gaps (paywall, bot wall, robots.txt, HTTP error, empty page). Call it before answering. Takes no parameters.

Web search through SearXNG ( OSTLER_SEARXNG_URL ) or Brave ( OSTLER_SEARCH_PROVIDER=brave and OSTLER_BRAVE_API_KEY ). Returns titles, URLs and snippets; a snippet is not evidence until the page is read. parameter type notes query string, required limit integer default 8, max 20 recency day | week | month | year site string host name, for example example.com

Read up to 10 URLs in a scratch tab; the agent's current tab is untouched. The domain policy is checked before robots.txt is fetched, robots.txt (RFC 9309) is obeyed, requests to one host are spaced, and the call has a time budget. Each page's outcome is reported. parameter type notes urls string array, required query string best passages from each page k integer passages per page, default 2, max 5 force boolean re-read pages already read

Structured data from the current page: tables as rows, or lists of repeated cards with pagination hints and a completeness verdict ( PARTIAL: 5 of 13 when the page states a total it does not show). parameter type notes kind tables | lists , required max_rows integer per table or list, default 30 where string keep only rows containing any of a|b|c select array table columns to keep, by header name or index

Links on the current page with anchor text and context, optionally filtered. parameter type notes same_origin boolean text_contains string href_contains string limit integer default 30 where string keep only lines containing any of a|b|c

Run a short Rhai script for multi-page jobs. Loops, filtering and counting happen outside the context; only the script's printed lines and final value come back, inside the untrusted fence. In the script, tool("read", #{url: u, query: "price"}) runs any Ostler tool and returns its text; grep(text, word) , lines(text) and print(x) help. No files, network, modules or eval ; at most 60 tool calls; every call keeps the profile, allowlist, robots.txt and submit-gate rules, and run cannot call run . See ADR-0019 . parameter type notes script string required max_chars integer default 8000
List the page's forms as typed fields (label, kind, required, options, errors) plus submit controls and what memory knows about this form. parameter type notes form string form ref

A value written {{fact:KEY}} is replaced by the saved fact with that key, so the value never has to pass through the agent. An unknown key fails the call. Fill many fields at once from {label | name | ref: value} . Handles selects, radios, checkbox groups, dates, files, comboboxes and dependent dropdowns, and verifies each field by reading it back. auto: "required" or "all" fills the rest from memory. parameter type notes values object {label | name | ref: value} form string form ref auto off | required | all fill the rest from memory min_confidence number The report names each field OK , or says UNMATCHED (no field matches the key), ambiguous (several match equally well, so use the ref), or

a read-back mismatch. It lists fields still empty and required, and says unsettled (a count) when the page was still busy at the end of the fill. File fields are refused unless --upload-dir allows the directory.

Click the form's submit or next control and report whether it was accepted, advanced to another step, or failed validation. parameter type notes form string control string submit button ref confirm boolean required when the server runs with --require-confirm-submit Result: Submitted , Advanced (next step), NOT ACCEPTED with the page's own messages, or Nothing changed when the form stays put and says nothing. Just before clicking it re-reads the fields it verified and reports any the page cleared or rewrote ( CHANGED BEFORE SUBMIT ).
Set one field by ref (any kind, including custom widgets). parameter type notes ref string, required value any, required
These need memory enabled ( --memory local , a Qdrant URL, or --memory ephemeral ). See Memory and privacy .

Save a fact about the user for future forms (for example email, company). Secrets are refused. parameter type notes key string, required value any, required description string autocomplete string HTML autocomplete token, for example given-name
Semantic search over saved facts. parameter type notes query string, required limit integer
List all saved facts. Takes no parameters.
Delete a saved fact by key. parameter type notes key string, required
Session cost and latency counters: calls, milliseconds, estimated tokens, browser memory. Takes no parameters.

Observation is part of the action. navigate returns the interactive elements; clicks and typing return only what changed. observe: none opts out but still records a baseline. Actions are never replayed after a navigation. Calls that change the page report that the page changed instead of re-running. A crashed Chrome is relaunched and the agent is told. Open tabs and page state are lost.

The threat model: what Ostler does, and what it does not do. This page is the repository's SECURITY.md . For how the memory-related rows work in practice, see Memory and privacy . Ostler lets an AI agent drive a real browser and stores some user data. Treat it like any tool that can act on your behalf.
Pre-1.0: only the latest released minor version (currently 0.2.x) and main receive security fixes.

Please use GitHub's private vulnerability reporting for this repository ("Security" tab → "Report a vulnerability"). Do not open a public issue for something exploitable. There is no bounty. This is a pre-1.0 project maintained by individuals. Include the version, how you ran it (flags, transport), and a minimal reproduction. What to expect, on a best-effort basis: We acknowledge the report as quickly as we can. We confirm and assess the impact, and tell you if we disagree it is a vulnerability. We prepare a fix privately, release it, and publish an advisory crediting you unless you prefer otherwise. Please keep the details private until a fix is released; we ask for coordinated disclosure
and will not rush you if you need time either.

The Security workflow ( .github/workflows/security.yml ) runs on every push to main , every pull request and weekly: cargo deny with deny.toml : RustSec advisories and yanked crates, an allow-list of licenses, wildcard version requirements, and sources (crates.io only; no git dependencies). Duplicate versions of a crate are reported as warnings, not failures. cargo audit --deny warnings : Cargo.lock against the RustSec database, including unmaintained and unsound warnings. Dependabot ( .github/dependabot.yml ) opens weekly grouped updates for Cargo dependencies and GitHub Actions. These cover known-vulnerable and disallowed dependencies. They do not detect unknown vulnerabilities, malicious
but unreported crates, or flaws in Ostler's own code. Workflows use read-only tokens, do not use pull_request_target , and pin actions by tag, not by commit SHA.

threat what we do what we do not do Prompt injection from a web page Page-derived text is wrapped in <page_content untrusted="true"> : page content, but also titles, URLs, dialog text and the look legend, which used to sit on trusted lines. Text a person cannot see (opacity 0, zero font size, far off-screen, same colour as the background) is left out and counted, so a hidden instruction never reaches the model. Server instructions tell the model not to follow page text. We cannot stop a model from being persuaded by text a person can also see. Hidden-text detection judges colour only against a solid background; gradients, images and clip -style screen-reader text are not treated as hidden.

Use --allow-domain and --require-confirm-submit for anything sensitive. Agent navigates somewhere it should not Domain allowlist enforced inside the browser. Every request the page makes is held and checked whatever its type (documents, images, stylesheets, scripts, fetch /XHR, beacons, event streams), and Chrome is started with a resolver rule that makes every other host unresolvable, which also covers WebSockets and the first request of a popup. Entries may pin a port ( example.com:8443 ). Only http(s); file: needs --allow-file . Tested with a canary server on a non-allowlisted origin: no request arrives through , a stylesheet, fetch , XHR, a beacon, a WebSocket, EventSource , a form

POST, a redirect, a meta refresh, a script navigation or window.open , by hostname or by IP literal. With no allowlist, --block-private-networks refuses loopback, private, link-local (cloud metadata), CGNAT and internal-looking hosts, and names that resolve to them. Independently of that flag, navigating to a literal link-local address (169.254.0.0/16 including 169.254.169.254, fe80::/10 , fd00:ec2::254 ) or a well-known metadata hostname ( metadata.google.internal ) is refused unless you allowlist it. An entry without a port allows every port on that host. Ports are checked on the requests interception sees; the browser-wide resolver rule works on hosts only, so treat a port pin as defence

in depth, not isolation, for WebSockets. The private-network check resolves a name before Chrome does, so a DNS-rebinding server can answer differently the second time: use an allowlist where that matters. --block-private-networks is off by default for serve because coding agents browse local dev servers (and the demo fixtures live on loopback); it is on by default for a2a . The always-on metadata check covers navigations and literal addresses only: without an allowlist, a page's own sub-requests and names that merely resolve to a metadata address are not checked. Not a sandbox against a compromised browser. Irreversible submissions --require-confirm-submit blocks every non-GET request

unless it happens inside form_submit with confirm=true . Off by default. A GET with side effects, and WebSockets, are not covered. The first request of a popup window and requests from cross-site iframes (their own browser processes) are covered too: Chrome is told to hold such targets at start ( Target.setAutoAttach with waitForDebuggerOnStart ) and interception is switched on before they are released, so --allow-domain host:port pins and the gate apply to them (tested with a canary: popup POST, popup GET to another port, cross-site iframe POST/ fetch /image). A submit that is cancelled mid-flight now closes the gate again. At most 8 popups are adopted (the rest are closed before they run).

A popup opened by the form you confirmed inherits the confirmation for its first request only, so a hostile page that opens a window during a confirmed submit can let that popup's first request through. File exfiltration through an upload field File fields are refused unless you pass --upload-dir DIR . A path is resolved first ( .. and symlinks included) and must land inside an allowed directory; the browser is handed the resolved path. Anything inside an allowed directory can be attached to any page the agent visits, so keep it small and free of secrets. A page's own "are you sure?" dialog confirm() and prompt() are dismissed, so a site's "Delete everything?" is not confirmed by a browser

nobody is watching, and the agent is told what happened. alert() and beforeunload are acknowledged. --accept-dialogs restores auto-accept for sites that need it. A dismissed confirm can leave a flow stuck; the agent sees the dialog text and can ask you. A remote agent over A2A Loopback by default; bearer token required to listen elsewhere; Origin and Host checks against browser-based attacks; per-conversation browsers; submit needs an explicit confirm; private and internal addresses are refused unless you pass --allow-private-networks . No TLS (use a reverse proxy). All conversations share one memory tenant. Always pass --allow-domain . See docs/A2A.md . Secrets in memory The memory API

refuses password/token/card-like keys and card-number-like values; sensitive fields are never auto-filled from memory nor stored by --learn ; sensitive values are masked in tool output; playbooks store structure only, never values. Detection is heuristic (names, autocomplete tokens, digit patterns). A secret stored under an innocuous key with an innocuous value will not be caught. Cross-user data exposure Every memory point carries a tenant ; every query filters on it; isolation is tested on a real Qdrant. With --isolation collection each tenant has its own collections and ostler memory token mints a JWT Qdrant itself limits to them (tested on Qdrant 1.20: other tenants answer 403). The

default shares collections, so a leaked admin key exposes every tenant. Collection isolation needs jwt_rbac and an admin who creates the collections. Someone who can read your Qdrant (operator, leaked key, backup) Payloads are sealed on your machine (AES-256-GCM); site names, labels, keys and point ids are keyed hashes; episodes are redacted of emails and numbers; plain http:// to a remote Qdrant is refused. The vector is not hidden: with --embeddings cloud the field text is sent to Qdrant Cloud Inference, and vectors of labels reveal roughly what they say. Use --embeddings ollama to keep text local. Tenant name, win/loss counters, timing and point counts stay visible. The key is a file or

env var by default (optionally the macOS Keychain or Linux Secret Service via key_store = keychain ). Lose it and sealed memory is unreadable; serve refuses to start rather than silently replace a key that cannot open existing memory, and a first start only creates a key after Qdrant was seen to hold no sealed memory for the tenant (with Qdrant unreachable it refuses unless you pass --allow-new-key ). Sealed blobs in the old v1 format are not read (run ostler memory seal once to upgrade them). Two simultaneous first starts on the Linux keychain are serialised by a lock file, which does not cover other programs writing the same Secret Service item; that path is tested against a scripted fake

secret-tool , not a real keyring. Malicious page attacking the runtime The injected runtime avoids eval and never executes page-supplied strings; it works on DOM objects. It runs before page scripts and keeps its own references to fetch , XMLHttpRequest and setTimeout . The runtime shares a JS world with the page, so a hostile page can replace window.__wm , patch Element.prototype / Array.prototype / JSON / Map after load, or read the runtime's functions, and so mislead what the agent is told (a field's value, whether something is visible or required) or how long a fill waits. Running it in a CDP isolated world was investigated and is not done: the activity tracking that settle depends on

works by patching fetch , XHR and timers in the page's own world, which an isolated world cannot do, and the same-origin-iframe walk calls the other frame's __wm . Doing it needs a split into a small main-world tracker and an isolated-world runtime ( ADR-0004 ). Page DOM content itself is always attacker-controlled; do not rely on the runtime for adversarial pages. Local exposure Chrome is launched with a throwaway profile and talks to Ostler over a pipe ( --remote-debugging-pipe ). There is no debugging port, so no other local user can connect to the browser, and Chrome exits by itself if Ostler dies. Tested: no listening socket in the browser's process tree (the WebSocket mode shows one).

OSTLER_CDP_TRANSPORT=ws brings back the old unauthenticated localhost port, for debugging only. With --profile-dir your logged-in sessions live on disk, readable by your own account and by any process running as you. Not audited. No security review has been done by a third party.

Qdrant (your cluster): facts you saved, form playbooks (field labels and which fact filled them), episodes (error messages from forms), all tagged with your tenant. By default these are encrypted before upload ( --seal ); the key is memory.key beside your config file or OSTLER_MEMORY_KEY . Disk: nothing by default; a Chrome profile only if you pass --profile-dir . Telemetry: none. ostler memory wipe --yes deletes everything for a tenant.

Let other agents hand Ostler forms over Agent2Agent v1.0. Ostler can be driven by another agent over A2A (v1.0, JSON-RPC over HTTP, SSE streaming), as well as by a coding agent over MCP. Use MCP when one agent owns the browser; use A2A when another agent (or service) should be able to hand Ostler a form as a task. ostler a2a --allow-domain example.com # http://127.0.0.1:8765 curl http://127.0.0.1:8765/.well-known/agent-card.json Ostler is a tool, not a language model . It understands structured requests, not free text. It tells a client so (it answers chatter with a message that shows the expected shape).

Send SendMessage (or SendStreamingMessage ) with a data part: { "url" : "https://example.com/signup" , "values" : { "Email" : "ada@example.com" , "Country" : "Germany" }, "submit" : true} field meaning url page to open first. Omit to continue on the conversation's current page values {label | name | ref: value} , filled and verified by reading each field back auto required or all : fill the rest from the owner's saved profile (needs Qdrant memory) submit submit once everything is filled and verified confirm the caller agrees to the submission No values , no auto , no submit : it just inspects the form. A bare URL in a text part does the same.

state when what the client does TASK_STATE_COMPLETED inspected, filled, or submitted and accepted read the artifacts TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED required fields missing, a key matched nothing or was ambiguous, the page rejected a value, a wizard advanced, or it is waiting for {"confirm": true} reply on the same taskId with more values or confirm TASK_STATE_FAILED blocked by policy, timed out, or the page never accepted the submit read the result artifact TASK_STATE_CANCELED CancelTask Nothing is submitted until the caller says confirm: true , unless the server runs with --a2a-auto-submit . A remote agent can of course just send it; the point is that a human-in-the-loop client has a place to

stop. Each task has two artifacts: result (compact text) and data (the same information as JSON: missing , unmatched , fieldErrors , …). Both are marked metadata.untrusted: true because they contain text from the website. Treat them as data, never as instructions.

One A2A contextId is one Ostler session: its own Chrome, its own tabs , and its own shared context notes. Messages with the same contextId (or the same taskId ) continue where the last one stopped, e.g. the form that was filled is still open when {"confirm": true} arrives. Different contextId s can never see each other's pages. Each conversation is a Chrome process (about 400-650 MiB), so it is capped: --max-contexts (default 4), idle ones are closed after --idle-secs (default 300).

SendMessage , SendStreamingMessage , GetTask , ListTasks , CancelTask , SubscribeToTask . GetExtendedAgentCard and the push-notification methods return the A2A errors for "not supported" ( -32007 , -32003 ). Errors use the A2A codes ( -32001 task not found, -32002 not cancelable, -32004 unsupported operation, -32009 version not supported) with a google.rpc.ErrorInfo detail. A2A-Version must be 1.x if sent. A missing header is accepted (the spec says to assume 0.3, which this server does not implement, so being lenient here is a deliberate choice).

The HTTP front door is bounded so a slow, greedy or abusive client cannot exhaust the machine. These are fields of A2aConfig (defaults shown). Only those with a flag shown have one today; the rest are library defaults until ostler a2a exposes them. Setting ( A2aConfig ) Default Behaviour max_body_bytes 1 MiB Larger request bodies get HTTP 413 (checked against Content-Length , and while reading chunked bodies). header_read_timeout 10 s Time to send a request's headers; also the idle limit on a kept-alive connection. The connection is closed on expiry (slowloris). body_timeout 15 s Time to send the body once headers are in. HTTP 408 on expiry. request_timeout 150 s Ceiling on handling a

request until its response starts (SSE streams continue afterwards). Raised to task_timeout + 15 s if lower, so a blocking SendMessage is never cut short. HTTP 408 . max_concurrent_tasks 8 Tasks running, or queued behind their conversation's turn. Over the limit: HTTP 429 , Retry-After: 5 , error reason TOO_MANY_TASKS_IN_FLIGHT . Nothing is queued without bound. max_contexts ( --max-contexts ) 4 Concurrent conversations (one Chrome each). Over the limit: HTTP 503 , Retry-After: 15 , reason TOO_MANY_CONTEXTS . task_timeout ( --task-timeout-secs ) 120 s One task; it then fails with "The task timed out." idle ( --idle-secs ) 300 s Idle conversations are closed. drain_timeout 30 s See shutdown

below. 429/503 responses are JSON-RPC errors (code -32603 ) with error.data[0].metadata.retryAfterSeconds , plus the Retry-After header. Clients should back off and retry. Probes (no auth, no Host check, body is only a status word; nothing about the host, paths or versions): GET /healthz : 200 {"status":"ok"} while the process is serving. GET /readyz : 200 {"status":"ready"} when the server is not shutting down and a Chrome binary can be found ( chrome_path , else the usual discovery order); otherwise 503 {"status":"not_ready"} . It checks that a browser can be located, not that a launch succeeds. Request ids. Every response has an X-Request-Id header. A client-supplied X-Request-Id (up to

64 characters of A-Za-z0-9-_. ) is echoed; otherwise a UUID is generated. Error bodies repeat it: requestId in the plain-JSON auth/host/timeout errors and error.data[0].metadata.requestId in JSON-RPC errors. Quote it when reporting a problem. Graceful shutdown. On SIGTERM or SIGINT the server stops accepting connections, /readyz turns 503, new tasks are refused with 503 ( SHUTTING_DOWN ), and in-flight requests and tasks get up to drain_timeout to finish. Anything still running is then aborted, every browser is closed, and the process exits. Set your orchestrator's termination grace period above drain_timeout . Not limited here: the number of open connections. Put a reverse proxy or firewall
in front for connection-level limits.

An A2A endpoint lets a network client steer a browser that can log in to things. Defaults are conservative: Binds 127.0.0.1 . Binding anything else requires --a2a-token (or OSTLER_A2A_TOKEN ); the server refuses to start otherwise. With a token, the RPC endpoint needs Authorization: Bearer … (compared in constant time). The Agent Card stays public, as the protocol expects, and advertises the scheme but never the token. Requests carrying an Origin header (a web page in a browser) are refused, and the Host header must be a loopback name or one you list with --allowed-host / --public-url . This blocks drive-by and DNS-rebinding attacks from a page open on the same machine. Always set

--allow-domain . Without it, any remote agent can send this browser to any public website. The allowlist is enforced inside the browser for every conversation (every request type, WebSockets included). Without an allowlist the server blocks loopback, private and cloud-metadata addresses so a remote agent cannot probe this machine's network ( --allow-private-networks turns that off); the server warns at startup. Uploads are refused unless you pass --upload-dir . TLS is not terminated here. Put it behind a reverse proxy for anything beyond localhost, and set --public-url . All conversations share one Qdrant tenant . If different callers must not see each other's saved profile, run one server
per tenant.

The official A2A Python SDK ( a2a-sdk 1.3.0) resolved the card, selected the JSON-RPC interface, streamed a three-turn conversation (input-required, input-required, completed) and received artifacts on every turn against the real binary. That was a manual check; the repository's own tests ( crates/ostler-a2a/tests ) use plain HTTP. Not implemented: gRPC and REST bindings, push notifications, extended cards, signed cards, and the v0.3 wire format.

t: Each has an ADR in docs/adr/ where the alternatives are written down. An injected runtime instead of CDP's accessibility tree. The cost: it is our code running in a hostile page's world, so it is written defensively (no eval , no page-supplied selectors executed as code) and it cannot see closed shadow roots or cross-origin frames. dropdowns, and seven tasks that must be refused (CAPTCHA, wrong format, server rejection, disabled control, unknown field, terms that stay disabled, username taken). Nothing is scraped; the pages are written from knowledge of those patterns. Every task has a ground-truth final state, and success is judged by what the fixture server received , never by what the tool said. A wrong value, or a "Submitted" that the server did not see, is a wrong-fill ; the suite exits non-zero on any. run pass correctly refused failed honestly wrong-fills first run, 27 tasks, before fixes 17 6 3 1 after fixes, 30 tasks 23 7 0 0 Read that honestly: the suite was written by the people who fixed what it found, so
