Unit costs, scaling limits, the moat question and what could go wrong. Written as the questions a skeptical investor or senior engineer would ask, answered with what we measured ( BENCHMARKS.md ) and clearly separated from what we assume. Where we do not know, we say so.

s: 1. What does one task cost, and who pays for what?
t: For a typical form task (measured on fixtures; LLM price is an illustrative $3 / $15 per Mtok): cost line per task share basis LLM tokens (3 calls, prompt-cached) ~$0.017-0.024 >99% measured token counts x illustrative price Browser compute ~$0.000006 ~0.03% measured 0.5 CPU-s + 0.5 GiB for ~1 s, illustrative cloud price Qdrant (memory ops) ~2 requests, sub-ms negligible measured; Cloud Inference model cost not measured Implication: the browser is not the cost center, the model is. A browser that is 2x faster or cheaper to run changes the bill by nothing. A browser that makes the agent take fewer turns and read fewer tokens changes it a lot: on a 20-field form we measure 5.0x lower LLM cost

s: 1. What does one task cost, and who pays for what?
t: and 5.4x lower latency than a per-field interaction pattern. Ostler's economic claim is therefore "fewer turns and fewer tokens per completed form", not "faster browser".

s: 2. Is the saving real, or an artefact of the baseline?
t: Partly baseline. The "per-field" comparison models the worst-case pattern (one call per field, full snapshot after each). Tools with batched fills close part of the gap. What stays differentiated even against a batched filler: verification by read-back, dependent dropdown/wizard handling in one call, shadow DOM/iframes, validation-error reporting, and cross-session memory. We do not yet have a head-to-head against other products on the same tasks; that is on the roadmap and we will publish it either way.

Per node (measured, 8-core laptop): 8 parallel sessions gave 354-393 tasks/min, p95 under 1 s, 100% success, flat latency, 450-550 MiB per session. Derived planning numbers, assuming CPU-bound at 0.5 CPU-s per task: ~7,000 tasks per core-hour; memory-bound at ~0.5 GiB per session: ~14 concurrent sessions per 8 GB, ~120 per 64 GB. Assumptions: Linux numbers will differ; real sites are heavier than fixtures (more CPU, more RAM per page); idle sessions hold memory. Treat as a first-order estimate until the Linux benchmark job reports. Memory layer (measured on real Qdrant): retrieval latency stays ~0.4 ms p50 from 20k to 200k points because queries are tenant-scoped via a payload index.

Throughput ~2.4-2.9k QPS with 16 clients on one laptop-hosted node. What does not scale yet (be skeptical here): Qdrant RAM per user is the open number. We saw ~6.8-8.4 KB per point at 200k points untuned, i.e. ~130-160 KB per user at 20 facts. At 1M users that is ~130-160 GB untuned. It is a loaded-and-queried figure, not isolated steady state, so it is an upper-ish bound, but it needs a proper sizing study with quantization and on-disk vectors before any capacity claim. Hosted multi-tenant browsers (isolation, anti-abuse, residential proxies, CAPTCHAs) are not built and are where hosted-browser companies spend most of their cost.

s: 4. What are the unit economics of a business around this?
t: This repository is an open-source tool (Apache-2.0), not a business. The plausible shapes, with their honest weaknesses: Pull-through for Qdrant Cloud. Weakness: low revenue per seat. Hosted sessions (managed browsers with memory). Compute is cheap (section 1), so gross margin is high before proxies, CAPTCHAs and abuse handling, which is where margin disappears. Weakness: crowded, and the hard costs are the ones we have not built. Enterprise (audit log, policy, SSO, approval workflows, on-prem).

Ostler is a form-filling browser for an agent working on your behalf, on one machine. It is the wrong tool when: The site walls off automation. CAPTCHA, Cloudflare/Turnstile, "verify you are human" pages and search-engine bot checks are reported with a CHALLENGE: line and handed to a person. Ostler never solves or bypasses them, and it is not built to avoid detection: there is no stealth patching, fingerprint spoofing, residential proxy or IP rotation. A site that blocks headless or datacenter Chrome will block Ostler. --headed plus a persistent --profile-dir lets you pass a check once; it does not make a bot wall go away. You need scale. Each server drives one local Chrome (tabs share its

cookies and profile). It is not a remote or cloud browser farm, not a crawler, and not meant for bulk scraping or high-volume account creation. More sessions means more servers, each with its own profile and its own memory use (see Benchmarks ). The flow needs an identity Ostler does not have. There is no mailbox, phone number, SMS/OTP receiver or authenticator: one-time codes, email-link verification, passkeys, hardware keys and 2FA prompts need a person. Passwords and card numbers are never read back or remembered; sensitive fields are refused and the agent is told to ask you. It does not create accounts on your behalf out of thin air. The page is outside what the injected runtime can see.

Cross-origin iframes (many hosted card fields), closed shadow roots, canvas-drawn UIs, native OS dialogs and file pickers, and desktop apps are not reachable. A control that stays disabled until a person scrolls or hovers is reported as disabled rather than worked around. A wrong submit is expensive and nobody is checking. Ostler verifies every value by reading it back and refuses to call a submit a success without evidence, but it cannot know whether a form means what it says. For payments, legal acceptance and anything irreversible, run with --require-confirm-submit and review the result yourself. When Ostler cannot finish, it says which field and why (rejected value with the page's own
message, hidden or disabled control, key not found) and points at screenshot for the element; it does not report a partial fill as done.

Ostler drives a real Chrome, but from a fresh, headless session many sites treat it as a bot. What to expect (it varies by network and over time): Google, DuckDuckGo, Brave, Startpage, Reddit, news sites such as the NYT: often a bot wall or CAPTCHA. Ostler reports it and hands off to a person; it never tries to solve or get around it. Bing: usually loads (but it may ignore first= / "Page 2" and serve page 1 again to a headless session), but may return results unrelated to your query ("Some results have been removed"). When a search-results URL's visible text matches fewer than about half of the query's words, navigate adds Warning: results do not seem to match the query "..." . Treat the

results as unreliable and try another engine or --headed . What helps, honestly: Run --headed with a persistent --profile-dir , one profile per server (Chrome locks a profile while it is in use). A person clears a CAPTCHA or signs in once in the visible window; cookies persist for later runs. When the agent hits a wall it calls wait_for_human : it pauses, you solve the page in the window, and it resumes from the same page. For pure discovery (finding which pages to read), use a search API; it is more reliable than scraping a results page. Ostler is best at reading the pages you already have URLs for and at filling forms. Do not spoof the user agent or try to hide automation; it is unreliable
and not something Ostler supports. If it still fails, open an issue with the output of ostler doctor and your OS and Chrome version.
